topic: The unread Voynich manuscript obeys Zipf's law like a real language, yet its glyph sequences are unusually predictable, unlike every comparison text.
summary: Beinecke MS 408, the Voynich manuscript, is about 240 pages of an unidentified script. Nobody can read it, but its statistics can be counted. Word frequencies fall off with rank as Zipf's law predicts, word lengths and vocabulary size look like those of ordinary languages, and keywords cluster by section. At the level of single glyphs, though, the text is unusually predictable: its conditional character entropy is unusually low, it differs from every comparison text studied, and reshuffling the glyph inventory does not bring it in line with natural languages.

facts.claim: The Beinecke Library catalogues the manuscript as Beinecke MS 408 and describes it as produced in Central Europe at the end of the fifteenth or during the sixteenth century.
facts.source_title: The Beinecke Cipher (Voynich) Manuscript | Yale Library

facts.claim: The manuscript has about 240 pages and roughly 38,000 words, of which about 9,000 are distinct.
Radiocarbon dating at the University of Arizona in 2009 placed the parchment between 1404 and 1438.

The most frequent word appears roughly twice as often as the second most common and three times as often as the third, following Zipf's law; the mix of word lengths and the ratio of distinct to total words resemble natural languages.
A script of 20 to 25 characters accounts for virtually all of the text, and there is no obvious punctuation.

Lindemann and Bowern found Voynichese conditional character entropy unusually low; substantial manipulations of glyph composition did not bring it in line with natural languages, and it was distinct from every comparison text.
facts.source_title: Character Entropy in Modern and Historical Texts: Comparison Metrics for an Undeciphered Manuscript (arXiv:2010.14697)

facts.claim: Montemurro and Zanette's information-theoretic analysis found an organisation of words compatible with real language, with informative keywords tied to the manuscript's sections.
facts.source_title: Keywords and Co-Occurrence Patterns in the Voynich Manuscript: An Information-Theoretic Analysis

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Zipf rank-frequency decay
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Sort the words by how often they occur. The count of the word at rank r is roughly proportional to 1/r, so the second word appears half as often as the first and the third a third as often.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Words or bars sized 1, 1/2, 1/3 and so on, or a log-log line of rank against count.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Low conditional glyph entropy
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Given one glyph, the next is easier to guess in Voynichese than in natural languages, so the text carries fewer bits per character even though its words behave normally.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: A letter stream where each next glyph is drawn from a narrow fan of likely successors, compared against a wider fan for a natural language.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Section-clustered keywords
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Some words concentrate in particular sections (herbal, astronomical, balneological) instead of spreading evenly, as topic words do in ordinary books.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Words gathering into separate regions by section while common words stay spread across all of them.

open_questions: Is the low character entropy caused by the transcription alphabet, by a cipher or by an unusual writing system?
Can a text generated by a simple copying procedure reproduce both the Zipf curve and the keyword clustering?

surprise.justification: The manuscript is famous, but the split verdict is not: word-level statistics look like language, glyph-level statistics look like nothing else measured.
